blocks.text: 8.3.3. Benefits of DRY for Concurrency

Each code of the spring campaign may be redeemed three times. A week after launch, finance finds codes redeemed four and five times. The web checkout reads how often a code was used and, if that is under the limit, adds one, so two orders that read at the same moment both pass. The team makes the web checkout check and update in one atomic step, its load test goes from oversold to clean, and the fix ships. The next week's report still shows oversold codes.
A Fix Made in One Copy of a Check-Then-Update Leaves the Other Copy Racing
The counters live in `PromoCodes`, which hands each checkout a code's counter:
The mobile checkout, which nobody looked at during the incident, has the same lines the web checkout had:

After its fix, the web checkout uses `getAndUpdate`, which stores the function's result only if no other thread changed the count in between, and retries otherwise. The function adds one only while the count is under the limit:

The load test releases eight threads together; each tries each of 20,000 codes once, in the same order; the mixed rows split the eight threads four and four. A code is oversold when more than three of its eight attempts succeed. Each row is 20 runs on fresh counters:

8 threads, 20000 codes, limit 3, 20 runs each
web, before its fix          20 of 20 runs oversold, worst run: 2905 codes
web, after its fix            0 of 20 runs oversold, worst run: 0 codes
mobile                       20 of 20 runs oversold, worst run: 3825 codes
web (fixed) and mobile       20 of 20 runs oversold, worst run: 2109 codes

The first two rows are the team's load test, which the fix passed. The mobile row is the same check-then-update, still racing. The last row is production: both checkouts share the codes, and the fixed web copy doesn't protect them. The mobile copy reads 2, a web order moves the counter to 3, and the mobile copy adds a fourth. This is the check-then-act of unit 6.2.1: each call is atomic, and the pair is not. On one thread nothing can come between the mobile copy's check and its update, so it refuses the fourth redemption too; only a test that runs several threads through the unfixed copy finds the race. With the incident closed, the next report's oversold codes look like a new bug.
A Fix Made in the Owning Class Reaches Every Caller Without Touching Them

Unit 8.3.2 shows how to move a compound action into the class that guards its state. Here `PromoCodes.tryRedeem` first held the mobile checkout's `get` and `incrementAndGet`, racing as before; after the fix it reads:
The checkouts never see a counter. Each is now one line, and `MobileCheckout` is the same class under another name:
The same load test, before and after the one edit to `tryRedeem`:

owner before its fix: 8 threads, 20000 codes, limit 3, 20 runs each
web                          20 of 20 runs oversold, worst run: 2524 codes
mobile                       19 of 20 runs oversold, worst run: 2489 codes
web and mobile               20 of 20 runs oversold, worst run: 2679 codes
owner after its fix: 8 threads, 20000 codes, limit 3, 20 runs each
web                           0 of 20 runs oversold, worst run: 0 codes
mobile                        0 of 20 runs oversold, worst run: 0 codes
web and mobile                0 of 20 runs oversold, worst run: 0 codes

Every row went to zero, mixed traffic included. javac produced the same bytes for `WebCheckout.class` and `MobileCheckout.class` before and after the fix, so a load test of `tryRedeem` covers every caller that only delegates to it.
**One machine.** Java 21, 20 cores, each program run three times: every racing row was oversold in 19 or 20 of its 20 runs, every fixed row in none.

`getAndUpdate` may call its function more than once when threads collide (unit 5.3.2), so the function only computes the new count; anything with a side effect, such as recording the order, goes after `tryRedeem` returns `true`.
<!-- practice 1 -->
The Fix Holds Only While No Caller Can Reach the Counter
A month later, a support tool needs to apply codes to phone orders, and its author pastes the redemption lines from an old branch of the mobile checkout:
Against the fixed `PromoCodes`:

pasted/SupportDesk.java:12: error: cannot find symbol
        AtomicInteger used = codes.counter(code);
                                  ^
  symbol:   method counter(String)
  location: variable codes of type PromoCodes
pasted/SupportDesk.java:13: error: cannot find symbol
        if (used.get() >= codes.limit()) return false;
                               ^
  symbol:   method limit()
  location: variable codes of type PromoCodes
2 errors

The public `counter()` of the first design is what made the copies possible: any class holding the `AtomicInteger` could write its own check-then-update, and nothing but review would stop it. With `counter()` gone, and `limit()`, which only the copies needed, the third copy fails to compile, and the author has to call `tryRedeem`.

Not every accessor reopens the race. A method `int redeemed(String code)` that returns the count as a number is safe to add: a caller may check it, but the only way to change the count is `tryRedeem`, which checks again.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Summary

items: **A fix made in one copy of a check-then-update leaves every other copy racing.** The fixed copy's own load test passes, and with mixed traffic the codes are still oversold.
**A fix made in the owning class reaches every caller without an edit to them.** One method and one load test cover every path; the callers compiled to the same bytes.
**The fix holds only while no caller can reach the state around the owner's method.** Return values, not the counter, and a pasted copy stops compiling.

blocks.text: Reference
**One call that validates and updates (Java 21 javadoc):**

rows: the function should be side-effect-free; it may be re-applied under contention
a per-key value in a map
the whole call is atomic and the function runs once; keep it short and simple, and don't modify the map from it
create a value once per key
atomic; the function runs at most once, only if the key is absent; keep it short and simple, and don't modify the map from it

blocks.text: Challenges

items: The redemption limit moves into a database that three services in different languages share. Where is the owner now, and what is the single step that validates and updates?
Finance adds a per-customer limit next to the per-code one. Can `tryRedeem` still be one atomic step, and what does keeping two counters consistent cost?
A code base has a dozen copies of a check-then-update against a shared cache. Which change tells you, with a compile, that you have found all of them?

blocks.text: Design Note: Why the Counter Is Hidden Rather Than Documented

The first design had a rule, "check and update a code's count in one step", that nothing in the code enforced. Hiding the counter moves the rule into the type: the only operation a caller has is the one that is correct.

The cost is that the owner must offer every compound action callers need. A checkout that wants "redeem these two codes together, or neither" can't build it from two `tryRedeem` calls; the owner needs a new method, and with it a lock or a single holder for both counts. Each such method makes the owner larger, and merging actions that only look alike has its own failure, which unit 8.3.4 shows.
